draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Across the PFAS adsorption studies represented in the supplied evidence, kinetic sampling strategies are structured to resolve both rapid early uptake and later-time approach to plateau or equilibrium, with specific time grids tuned to the system behavior rather than following a single universal schedule.

For adsorption of nine PFASs on powder-activated carbon (PAC) from surface water, Son et al. report that sorption kinetics were measured as removal efficiency versus time at 30, 60, 120, 240, 360, and 480 minutes at 10 mg/L PAC. They note that “the adsorption rate of all the PFASs was initially fast, indicating that ~70% of removal was accomplished within 30 min” and that for several PFASs “70–80% and 90% of the adsorption process was accomplished within 30 and 60 min, respectively.” This sampling grid, with multiple points in the first 1–2 hours, captures the rapid initial uptake phase. Later points out to 240–480 minutes are used to follow the system toward steady behavior: Son et al. state that “constant efficiency was observed at ~240 min” and that “the others required 360 min to reach 90% adsorption.” Thus, in this PAC system, kinetic sampling is dense enough at early times to quantify the fast initial removal and extended long enough to see the transition to a constant-efficiency regime and near-endpoint conditions, with different PFASs approaching 90% adsorption at different contact times.

In Militao et al.’s study of PFOS removal using alginate-encapsulated rice-straw biochar, the temporal pattern is resolved at the scale of hours. They report that “PFOS uptake was relatively fast with > 80 % of the adsorption achieved within the first 6 h followed by slow kinetics that plateaued within 16 h.” The description of an “initial fast adsorption stage” followed by “slow kinetics that plateaued” indicates that sampling covered the initial hours to capture rapid uptake and was extended to at least ~16 hours to observe the plateau. These data show a clear transition: most adsorption occurs in the early 6-hour window, while additional contact time mainly reveals a slowing approach to a plateau, which defines the endpoint for this system.

Chaudhary et al. examine PFAS (including PFOS and GenX) adsorption on regenerable carbonaceous adsorbents under mixed PFAS/Cd(II) conditions and likewise report distinct early and later kinetic regimes on the timescale of hours. They state that “PFOS displayed the fastest adsorption rate, reaching complete removal (10 mg g−1) within 2 h whereas GenX exhibited the slowest uptake reaching equilibrium after 6 h of reaction time.” Their discussion emphasizes that “the time required to reach the PFAS adsorption equilibrium is strongly dependent on the adsorbent properties.” To illustrate this dependence, they summarize literature where PFOS and PFOA adsorption on granular activated carbon (GAC) required 168 h for equilibrium, while powdered activated carbon (PAC) in another study gave equilibrium within 4 h for PFOS and PFOA; additional reports cited include equilibrium times of 24 h for PFOS, ~120 h for PFOA, and ~15 h for PFOA and PFOS on PAC. Together, these examples show that endpoint sampling in PFAS adsorption experiments can range from a few hours to several days, depending on adsorbent type and PFAS identity, and that kinetic experiments are typically continued until equilibrium or a clear plateau is reached for the specific system.

Taken as a whole, the evidence shows that PFAS kinetic experiments commonly employ early-time sampling that is fine-grained enough (minutes to a few hours) to capture rapid initial uptake phases, followed by extended sampling (hours to days) to characterize the transition to constant efficiency or plateaued adsorption. The transition from fast uptake to slower, plateau-like behavior is explicitly documented in multiple systems: ~70% removal in 30 minutes with constant efficiency at ~240 minutes on PAC; >80% PFOS removal within 6 hours and plateau by 16 hours on alginate-biochar; complete PFOS removal within 2 hours and GenX equilibrium at 6 hours on certain carbonaceous adsorbents; and equilibrium times from 4 to 168 hours in other GAC and PAC systems. These observations also demonstrate that both early uptake dynamics and endpoint timing depend strongly on adsorbent properties and PFAS-specific interactions, so the reported strategies illustrate principles for scheduling kinetic sampling but do not support a single fixed set of time intervals as universally applicable across all PFAS adsorption, removal, or degradation experiments.

draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Studies comparing PFAS treatment in simple versus real matrices consistently show that matrix composition can substantially change observed removal or degradation efficiencies, and that the direction and magnitude of the effect are system‑specific.

For nonthermal plasma–ozonation, Chen et al. report that in real wastewater the PFAS defluorination percentage is only "about 3 % lower in real wastewater" than in synthetic wastewater and that "the difference in results obtained in both matrices did not exceed 10 % in this study" (NQ20_MMG001). This indicates that for this particular reactor, matrix effects are present but modest.

In contrast, other systems show much stronger matrix inhibition. In photocatalytic degradation of PFOA and PFOS with Cs@g‑C3N4, El‑Sawaf et al. report that in deionized water the PFOA removal and apparent rate constant are 93 ± 1.5% and 0.0222 min⁻¹, and PFOS values are 88 ± 1.7% and 0.0177 min⁻¹, whereas in filtered river water the corresponding values drop to 72 ± 2.6% and 0.0106 min⁻¹ for PFOA and 68 ± 3.1% and 0.00950 min⁻¹ for PFOS (NQ20_MMG002). Thus, both removal and kinetics are substantially worse in the real river matrix than in DI water.

Chen et al. also evaluated plasma‑based degradation of PFOA in synthetic versus real landfill leachate. Under plasma alone, they found that "the degradation and defluorination efficiency of PFOA in real wastewater decreased by 22 % and 19 %, respectively, compared to synthetic wastewater" (NQ20_MMG003), and more generally that when comparing synthetic and real wastewater under standalone plasma or ferrate, "degradation performance was consistently better in synthetic wastewater" (NQ20_MMG004). Urtiaga et al. report an even more pronounced effect for electrochemical oxidation: the normalized kinetic constant for PFOA removal in real MBR‑treated landfill leachate is k′ₙ,PFOA = 0.238 h⁻¹ A⁻¹ L, which is "about 13 times lower" than in a synthetic mixed PFAS solution simulating groundwater and "26 times lower than for treating PFOA in a highly concentrated single compound solution" (NQ20_MMG006). They further cite Pierpaoli et al., who found that when landfill leachate is used as the background matrix, "the rates of PFOA degradation ... were reduced by one third to one-half" compared to a phosphate buffer electrolyte (NQ20_MMG008). These results show that real leachate matrices can slow electrochemical PFAS degradation by factors ranging from roughly 1.3 to more than 10 relative to simple synthetic electrolytes.

For sorbent‑based treatment, Parker et al. observed that both Biochar Basic and RemBind™ "gave decreased performance in heavy metal and PFAS removal from untreated OGSIR SW compared to simple synthetic stormwater" (NQ20_MMG005). The stormwater was characterized by salts, relatively high iron (210 µg L⁻¹), and organic matter, which "suggests that OGSIR SW constituents inhibit the sorbents' performance" (NQ20_MMG005). Thus, even when a sorbent performs well in a simple synthetic stormwater, actual field stormwater composition can impair PFAS removal.

Some advanced or combined processes can partly or fully overcome these matrix effects. In the nonthermal plasma‑ozonation cascade reactor, the fact that the real versus synthetic wastewater differences "did not exceed 10 %" (NQ20_MMG001) shows relatively robust performance against matrix complexity. In the plasma–ferrate system, Chen et al. note that plasma alone in real wastewater suffers an efficiency drop of about 20%, but that adding ferrate "oxidized and coagulated organics, mitigating their quenching effect on reductive species and restoring high degradation efficiency, resulting in PFOA removal comparable to that in synthetic wastewater (≈ 90 %)" (NQ20_MMG007). The same work reports that the combined plasma–ferrate process gave "similar degradation kinetics in real and synthetic wastewater, suggesting that the integrated process effectively overcame the inhibitory effects typically associated with real water matrices" (NQ20_MMG004), and that ferrate addition raised PFOA degradation efficiency in real wastewater to 91%, "comparable to that observed in synthetic wastewater (92 %)" (NQ20_MMG003).

Mechanistically, several matrix‑related phenomena are implicated. In the plasma systems, Chen et al. attribute the reduced PFOA degradation and defluorination in real wastewater primarily to "coexisting organic and inorganic compounds" that "act as scavengers of key plasma-generated reactive species, particularly eaq– and H•"; these reductive species are "essential for effective PFAS degradation, and their quenching by background matrix components hinders overall treatment performance" (NQ20_MMG003). They further explain that performance is better in synthetic wastewater because it lacks "complex matrix constituents such as natural organic matter, competing anions and metal ions that can scavenge reactive species or interfere with reaction pathways in real wastewater" (NQ20_MMG004). The beneficial effect of ferrate is attributed to its ability to oxidize and coagulate organics, thereby "mitigating their quenching effect on reductive species" and restoring high removal (NQ20_MMG007).

In sorption systems, Parker et al. link decreased PFAS removal in untreated stormwater to the presence of "salts, iron ... and organic matter" (NQ20_MMG005), suggesting that these constituents compete with PFAS for sorbent sites, alter surface charge, or otherwise inhibit sorbent performance compared with the simpler sodium–chloride–carbonate composition of the synthetic stormwater.

Electrochemical studies do not detail specific scavenging reactions in the provided excerpts, but the observed 6‑ to 26‑fold decreases in normalized kinetic constants and the one‑third to one‑half rate reductions when landfill leachate replaces simulated groundwater or phosphate buffer electrolytes (NQ20_MMG006, NQ20_MMG008) are consistent with real matrices introducing additional electroactive species, competing ions, or natural organic matter that interfere with PFAS oxidation pathways.

Overall, the evidence shows that real wastewater, landfill leachate, river water, and stormwater matrices can substantially alter PFAS treatment performance relative to DI water or simple synthetic solutions. These changes arise largely from scavenging of key reactive species and competition or inhibition by salts, natural organic matter, metals, and other co‑contaminants. Because the magnitude of these effects ranges from minor (<10%) to more than an order-of-magnitude decrease in apparent kinetic constants, performance measured in DI or simple synthetic matrices cannot be assumed to directly predict outcomes in real wastewaters or environmental waters without explicitly considering matrix effects for the particular process and matrix in question.
